Israeli Shekel Plunges to Record Lows, Sparking Economic Turmoil

JERUSALEM, June 12 — Israel’s currency plunged to record lows against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, sending shockwaves through the country’s economy as businesses and households grappled with soaring prices and mounting uncertainty.

The shekel fell more than 11% against the dollar in just two weeks, trading at 4.85 per dollar by midday, its weakest level since records began in the 1980s. Analysts attributed the collapse to a combination of political instability, a sharp drop in foreign investment, and rising concerns about government debt.

Market turmoil has already prompted the Bank of Israel to hold emergency meetings, with Governor Amir Yaron saying in a statement, “We are closely monitoring developments and stand ready to take measures necessary to ensure the stability of the financial system.” The central bank has not ruled out raising interest rates or intervening directly in currency markets.

Consumers have seen the immediate impact at supermarkets and fuel stations, where imported goods and energy costs have surged. The Manufacturers Association of Israel said more than 40% of its members are reporting disruptions to supply chains and difficulty securing foreign currency for purchases abroad.

Among the companies affected is ICL Group Ltd, a major player in the chemicals and minerals sector. “The sharp devaluation has significantly increased our input costs, particularly for materials and equipment sourced from overseas,” said Miriam Tal, a spokesperson for ICL Group Ltd. “We are reviewing all operations and may have to adjust our pricing and procurement strategies in the coming weeks.”

Other businesses, such as the electronics retailer TechSmart, have warned of possible price hikes and layoffs if the currency crisis persists. The Israel Chamber of Commerce urged the government to stabilize the situation swiftly, warning that “prolonged volatility could lead to recession and lasting economic damage.”

Economists say Israel’s strong tech sector and healthy foreign reserves provide some cushion, but uncertainty remains high. “The longer the shekel remains under pressure, the greater the risk to growth and employment,” said David Gelman, chief economist at Tel Aviv-based consultancy MacroView.

The Bank of Israel is expected to announce further steps later this week.
